old: Tiran and Sanafir are two Red Sea islands at the mouth of the Gulf of Aqaba, and Egypt agreed in April 2016 to hand them to Saudi Arabia. Tiran controls the shipping lane to the ports of Eilat in Israel and Aqaba in Jordan, and Egypt's closure of that lane helped cause the 1967 Arab-Israeli war. The Egyptian government says the islands were always Saudi and were put under Egypt's protection in the 1950s because of tensions with Israel. Critics link the transfer to billions of dollars of Saudi aid to the government of President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi and call it a sell-off of national territory. The announcement, during a visit by the Saudi king, set off the largest protests against the government since 2014, and hundreds of people were arrested. A court ruled against the transfer in January 2017. Politicians backing it argued that parliament had the right to ratify treaties, and on 14 June 2017, a day after police beat protesters in Cairo, parliament voted to ratify the agreement.
new: Tiran and Sanafir are two Red Sea islands at the mouth of the Gulf of Aqaba, and Egypt agreed in April 2016 to hand them to Saudi Arabia. Tiran controls the shipping lane to the ports of Eilat in Israel and Aqaba in Jordan, and Egypt's closure of that lane helped cause the 1967 Arab-Israeli war. The Egyptian government says the islands were always Saudi and were put under Egypt's protection around 1950 because of tensions with Israel. Critics link the transfer to billions of dollars of Saudi aid to the government of President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi and call it a sell-off of national territory. The announcement, during a visit by the Saudi king, set off the largest protests against the government since 2014, and hundreds of people were arrested. The Supreme Administrative Court ruled against the transfer in January 2017, but another court set that ruling aside in April, and the Constitutional Court later halted all rulings in the case. The head of parliament said it would not recognise any ruling on the agreement. On 14 June 2017, a day after police beat protesters in Cairo, parliament voted to approve it, and President Sisi ratified it on 24 June. A government report said the deal ended Egyptian sovereignty while Egypt kept administering the islands for the time being.
why: Ratification on 24 June 2017, later court history and the sovereignty clause now verified; date of Egyptian protection corrected from 1950s to around 1950 (sources give 1949 to 1950).

old: An Egyptian court ruled against the transfer in January 2017; street protests

old: The Rudd Concession was an 1888 agreement in which King Lobengula of Matabeleland, in what is now Zimbabwe, signed away the mineral rights of his kingdom to three men, Charles Rudd and Francis Thompson of Kimberley and Rochfort Maguire of London. The text promised him £100 every lunar month, 1,000 Martini-Henry rifles with 100,000 cartridges, and either a steamboat with guns on the Zambezi River or £500. In return the three men received complete and exclusive charge over all metals and minerals in his lands, and the power to do whatever they judged necessary to get them. The king also authorised them to keep out everyone else seeking land or mining rights, and agreed to grant no more concessions without their consent. The document says this was because rival concession seekers had been bothering him. A witness named Helm certified that the terms had been explained to the king and his council. The grant was to end if the monthly payment fell three months behind. In the years that followed, Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company held charter lands in the region and was expanding them northward.
new: The Rudd Concession was an 1888 agreement in which King Lobengula of Matabeleland, in what is now Zimbabwe, signed away the mineral rights of his kingdom to three men, Charles Rudd, Francis Thompson and Rochfort Maguire, who were agents of the businessman and politician Cecil Rhodes. Rhodes wanted to bring the region into the British Empire, and he needed the concession to win a charter for a company that could annex and govern it. The text promised him £100 every lunar month, 1,000 Martini-Henry rifles with 100,000 cartridges, and either a steamboat with guns on the Zambezi River or £500. In return the three men received complete and exclusive charge over all metals and minerals in his lands, and the power to do whatever they judged necessary to get them. The king also authorised them to keep out everyone else seeking land or mining rights, and agreed to grant no more concessions without their consent. The document says this was because rival concession seekers had been bothering him. A witness named Helm certified that the terms had been explained to the king and his council. From 1889 Lobengula tried to disown the deal, saying that limits agreed orally had been left out, and sent envoys to Queen Victoria, without success. Britain granted a royal charter to Rhodes's British South Africa Company in October 1889, and the company occupied Mashonaland in 1890. Its troops conquered Matabeleland in 1893 and 1894, and Lobengula died in exile soon afterwards. The company's charter ended in 1923, when Southern Rhodesia became a self-governing colony.
why: Rhodes link and outcome now verified.

old: The written deal covered minerals and the right to exclude rivals. It transferred no sovereignty and no land on its face, which shows how a narrow commercial grant can still shut a ruler out of dealing with anyone else.
new: The written deal covered minerals only and transferred no sovereignty, but it became the legal basis for a royal charter that let a company annex and govern the country. The king's objections did not stop it.
why: Earlier text stopped at the wording of the deal.

old: In September 2019 the provincial government of Central Province in the Solomon Islands signed an agreement giving a Chinese state-linked developer, China Sam Enterprise Group, exclusive development rights to the island of Tulagi and its neighbours. RNZ, the New Zealand public broadcaster, described it as a five-year lease deal. It came around the time the Solomon Islands opened diplomatic relations with China. The agreement spoke vaguely of trade, minerals, possible oil and gas, and a special economic zone. Local people and Western diplomats were alarmed, and one senior diplomat said that the wording could allow strategic assets such as deep-sea ports. In October the national Attorney-General, John Muria, said it was unlawful and unenforceable and must be terminated at once. It had not been vetted by his office as the law required, and an illegal clause would have exempted the company from foreign-investor rules. The provincial premier, Stanley Manetiva, said the deal was not legally binding and was no longer an issue.
